title: What would it take for dark matter to be literally warm?
summary: Warm dark matter (WDM) has served as a valuable benchmark for constraining small-scale structure in the past decades. In this note, I examine what it would take for dark matter to be warm in the literal sense assumed by that benchmark, i.e., a thermal relic that decoupled while relativistic. Satisfying current constraints on the WDM mass, which approach the $\sim$10 keV scale, requires one of three possibilities. One possibility is that there were $\sim 10^4$ relativistic degrees of freedom in the thermal bath at the time of decoupling, which is far beyond what is available in the Standard Model or plausible extensions of it. An alternative is that there was a period of early matter domination whose entropy injection diluted the relic density. However, in this scenario, the perturbations would have evolved through an expansion history that was different from the radiation-dominated one assumed in deriving WDM transfer functions. The third possibility is a dark sector that was never in thermal contact with the Standard Model and was simply born colder via asymmetric reheating. All of these possibilities rely on strong coincidences, where physics that has nothing to do with WDM happens to provide the exact initial conditions assumed in a WDM cosmology. Meanwhile, WDM is often used as a proxy for models with self-consistent thermal histories that generically predict the suppression of structure formation on small scales in a way that is both quantitatively and qualitatively different from WDM. I therefore advocate for a transition to more expressive parameterizations and simulation-based methods in order to extract more useful information from the wealth of upcoming data.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that Warm Dark Matter (WDM) as a thermal relic benchmark for constraining small-scale structure is theoretically implausible. Producing a ~10 keV WDM thermal relic requires either ~10^4 relativistic degrees of freedom, early matter domination with entropy injection, or asymmetric reheating of a dark sector—all requiring strong coincidences. The paper advocates shifting to more expressive parameterizations and simulation-based methods.
AI.motivation: WDM has been widely used as a benchmark for constraining small-scale structure, but the author examines the physical plausibility of dark matter being warm in the literal thermal-relic sense and finds it requires highly contrived conditions that do not naturally arise in realistic models.
AI.method: The paper systematically evaluates the three possible scenarios that could produce a ~10 keV WDM thermal relic: (1) ~10^4 relativistic degrees of freedom at decoupling, (2) early matter domination with entropy injection diluting relics, and (3) a dark sector born colder via asymmetric reheating. Each is examined for physical consistency and coincidence requirements.
AI.result: All three pathways to a keV-scale WDM thermal relic require strong coincidences where unrelated physics must provide exact initial conditions assumed in WDM cosmology. Additionally, the WDM proxy fails to capture the qualitatively and quantitatively different small-scale structure suppression predicted by models with self-consistent thermal histories.
AI.conclusion: The author advocates abandoning WDM as a benchmark in favor of more expressive parameterizations and simulation-based methods to better extract information from upcoming observational data.

title: Enhancing dark siren cosmology via Gaussian process reconstruction of incomplete galaxy catalogs
summary: We present a novel framework for improving dark siren cosmology by applying a Gaussian process (GP) to the line-of-sight (LOS) reconstruction of incomplete galaxy catalogs. In the standard galaxy catalog method for inferring the Hubble constant $H_0$ from gravitational-wave (GW) dark sirens, missing galaxies are typically assumed to follow a uniform distribution in comoving volume, an assumption that discards galaxy redshift clustering information crucial for cosmological inference. We propose instead to model the LOS galaxy redshift distribution as a non-parametric function drawn from a GP realization, which is fitted to the observed incomplete catalog via a hierarchical Bayesian likelihood that explicitly accounts for the survey selection function. Applied to mock GW and galaxy catalogs extending up to redshift $z\leq0.4$, our method yields $H_0$ constraints that are on average 23% more precise than the standard homogeneous completion when using a 24%-complete galaxy catalog, and 37% more precise for an 8%-complete catalog. The largest improvement, reaching 66%, is obtained in configurations where the GP most effectively reconstructs the redshift over- and under-density features that the homogeneous completion fails to capture.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a Gaussian process-based framework for reconstructing the line-of-sight galaxy redshift distribution from incomplete galaxy catalogs, improving dark siren Hubble constant inference. The method yields H0 constraints that are 23-66% more precise than the standard homogeneous completion approach.
AI.motivation: Standard galaxy catalog methods for inferring H0 from GW dark sirens assume missing galaxies follow a uniform comoving volume distribution, discarding crucial galaxy redshift clustering information needed for cosmological inference.
AI.method: The LOS galaxy redshift distribution is modeled as a non-parametric function from a Gaussian process realization, fitted to the observed incomplete catalog via a hierarchical Bayesian likelihood that explicitly accounts for the survey selection function.
AI.result: Applied to mock GW and galaxy catalogs up to z≤0.4, the method yields H0 constraints 23% more precise (24%-complete catalog), 37% more precise (8%-complete catalog), and up to 66% more precise when the GP best reconstructs redshift over-density and under-density features.
AI.conclusion: Modeling incomplete galaxy catalogs with Gaussian processes for LOS redshift reconstruction significantly outperforms the standard homogeneous completion assumption, particularly for highly incomplete catalogs where clustering information is most valuable.

title: Slowly Rolling on a Quantum Correction
summary: Recent advances in cosmological measurements such as DESI and ACT may indicate an increase in the preferred value of the spectral tilt $n_s$ such that it disfavors rather popular models such as the Higgs or Starobinski inflation models. We argue that it actually means that the data is now sensitive enough to quantum corrections beyond simple tree-level models. Resurrecting the old theme of Coleman-Weinberg effective potential, we analyze the predictions of such models, as well as likelihood analysis, leading to a more established and interesting predictive framework.

AI.tldr: Recent cosmological data (DESI, ACT) suggests a higher value of the spectral tilt n_s that disfavors popular inflation models like Higgs or Starobinski. The authors argue this indicates the data is now sensitive to quantum corrections beyond tree level, and they revive the Coleman-Weinberg effective potential approach to provide a more robust predictive framework.
AI.motivation: Recent cosmological measurements from DESI and ACT may favor a higher spectral tilt n_s, which disfavors popular inflation models such as Higgs or Starobinski inflation. This motivates re-examining whether quantum corrections, rather than the simple tree-level models, could explain the observed data and provide a better predictive framework.
AI.method: The authors revisit the Coleman-Weinberg effective potential approach to analyze the predictions of these models, and perform a likelihood analysis comparing the models against the new cosmological data.
AI.result: The analysis leads to a more established and interesting predictive framework that can accommodate the increased preferred value of the spectral tilt n_s indicated by the new data.
AI.conclusion: The apparent tension with popular inflation models is not a failure of these ideas but rather a signal that the data has become sensitive enough to quantum corrections beyond simple tree-level models. The Coleman-Weinberg effective potential framework provides a more robust and predictive alternative.

title: Quantifying the systematic impact of differential beam response on the BICEP CMB polarization data from 2016 through 2024
summary: As cosmic microwave background (CMB) polarization experiments, including BICEP3, BICEP Array, and future BICEP experiments, achieve ever-deeper polarization maps in search of primordial B-modes sourced from inflation, constraining instrumental systematics below statistical uncertainties becomes progressively more challenging. Since polarimetry in the BICEP telescopes is performed by pair-differencing co-located, orthogonally polarized detectors, differential beam response leads to temperature-to-polarization ($T \rightarrow P$) leakage, introducing a potential systematic bias on the inferred tensor-to-scalar ratio $r$. To mitigate this leakage, the lowest-order beam mismatch modes are filtered out of the CMB polarization maps through deprojection; however, residual undeprojected modes remain. To quantify this residual contamination, we perform dedicated in situ far-field beam measurements of the BICEP receivers during austral-summer calibration campaigns. We quantify the systematic impact of the undeprojected residuals with a specialized set of timestream simulations based on the measured per-detector beams. These "beam measurement-informed simulations" yield an estimate of the false polarized signal sourced by the undeprojected residuals. We summarize the beam measurements relevant to the BK24 data release and present preliminary residual-leakage results for BICEP3 at 95 GHz. For BICEP3 over 2016-2024, deprojecting all six standard templates together with readout-crosstalk templates and their radially smoothed counterparts reduces the equivalent-$r$ leakage amplitude from $ρ=(4.5\pm0.7)\times10^{-3}$ to $(1.12\pm0.06)\times10^{-3}$. We further describe an ongoing program to extend the deprojection basis beyond its historical six modes, guided by a forward optical model that relates candidate leakage modes to perturbations of physical instrument parameters.

AI.tldr: This paper quantifies the residual temperature-to-polarization leakage in BICEP3 CMB polarization maps caused by differential beam response, using in situ far-field beam measurements and timestream simulations. Deprojecting six standard templates plus readout-crosstalk templates reduces the equivalent-r leakage from ρ=(4.5±0.7)×10⁻³ to (1.12±0.06)×10⁻³ for 2016-2024 data.
AI.motivation: As BICEP experiments search for primordial B-modes via deeper CMB polarization maps, instrumental systematics must be constrained below statistical uncertainties. Differential beam response in pair-differenced detectors causes T→P leakage that can bias the tensor-to-scalar ratio r; quantifying and mitigating residual leakage after standard deprojection is essential.
AI.method: Dedicated in situ far-field beam measurements of BICEP receivers during austral-summer calibration campaigns are performed. Measured per-detector beams feed specialized timestream simulations ("beam measurement-informed simulations") to estimate false polarized signals from undeprojected residual modes. The deprojection basis is extended beyond the historical six standard templates by including readout-crosstalk templates and radially smoothed counterparts, guided by a forward optical model linking candidate leakage modes to physical instrument parameter perturbations.
AI.result: For BICEP3 at 95 GHz over 2016-2024, deprojecting all six standard templates together with readout-crosstalk templates and their radially smoothed counterparts reduces the equivalent-r leakage amplitude from ρ=(4.5±0.7)×10⁻³ to (1.12±0.06)×10⁻³.
AI.conclusion: The extended deprojection basis significantly suppresses residual beam-induced T→P leakage in BICEP3. An ongoing program to further expand the deprojection basis, informed by a forward optical model, promises additional improvements in systematics control for current and future BICEP experiments.

title: SMUDGes Below the Surface: Clusters Confirm the Diversity of Low-Surface-Brightness Galaxies
comment: Submitted to ApJ. 26 pages, 13 figures. Comments are welcome
summary: We use spatially resolved Keck Cosmic Web Imager spectroscopy to study high-surface-brightness stellar components and internal kinematics in 44 low-surface-brightness galaxies from the SMUDGes survey, including 30 ultradiffuse galaxies, spanning the red sequence, green valley, and blue cloud regions of the galaxy color-magnitude diagram. Although these galaxies appear largely smooth in survey imaging, we detect at least one cluster candidate in every galaxy. We identify clusters with nebular emission lines in 24 galaxies. They are common in blue-cloud galaxies but rare in red sequence galaxies. We identify three nuclear star cluster candidates, one of which shows nebular emission lines. Among clusters without nebular emission lines, bluer galaxies tend to have brighter cluster luminosity functions, suggesting the presence of young or intermediate-age clusters in addition to old globular clusters. This age diversity may complicate the use of photometrically selected globular cluster populations as tracers of total halo mass. We measure rotation velocities for 17 galaxies using the clusters with nebular emission lines and for 12 using diffuse stellar light. Within 0.5 effective radii, the inferred dynamical mass generally exceeds the stellar mass, although the inferred dark matter contribution varies by an order of magnitude. The variety in properties for this sample of ultradiffuse galaxies and low-surface-brightness dwarfs suggests that no single formation mechanism explains the population of low-surface-brightness galaxies.

AI.tldr: Using Keck Cosmic Web Imager spectroscopy, the authors study stellar clusters and internal kinematics in 44 low-surface-brightness galaxies (30 of which are ultradiffuse) from the SMUDGes survey. They detect cluster candidates in every galaxy, find young/intermediate-age clusters in bluer galaxies, measure rotation velocities for 17-29 galaxies, and conclude that no single formation mechanism explains the diverse properties of low-surface-brightness galaxies.
AI.motivation: Low-surface-brightness galaxies, including ultradiffuse galaxies, are poorly understood in terms of their stellar populations, cluster systems, and internal dynamics. The authors aim to characterize their formation mechanisms and assess whether globular clusters are reliable tracers of halo mass in these systems.
AI.method: Spatially resolved Keck Cosmic Web Imager spectroscopy of 44 SMUDGes low-surface-brightness galaxies (30 ultradiffuse). Detection of cluster candidates via imaging, identification of nebular-emission-line clusters, analysis of cluster luminosity functions by galaxy color, and measurement of rotation velocities from both nebular-line clusters and diffuse stellar light to infer dynamical masses.
AI.result: Cluster candidates detected in all 44 galaxies; emission-line clusters found in 24 galaxies (common in blue-cloud, rare in red sequence). Three nuclear star cluster candidates identified (one with emission lines). Bluer galaxies show brighter cluster luminosity functions, indicating age diversity. Rotation velocities measured for 17 galaxies via clusters and 12 via diffuse light. Dynamical mass within 0.5 effective radii exceeds stellar mass, but dark matter contribution varies by an order of magnitude.
AI.conclusion: The wide range of properties across the sample indicates that low-surface-brightness galaxies are not produced by a single formation channel. Additionally, the age diversity of clusters may complicate the use of photometrically selected globular cluster populations as tracers of total halo mass.

title: Cosmic topology. Part Va. Information content of the observable Universe
summary: If the Universe possesses a compact spatial topology with characteristic scale not much larger than the diameter of the observable Universe, then the associated symmetry transformations imprint specific statistical correlations on density perturbations. We derive the covariance between perturbation modes in the full topology volume and compute the induced covariance between modes in the observable subvolume. We then use this covariance to estimate the available information about topology contained in the full set of observable linear perturbations. For two sample Euclidean examples - the cubic three-torus ($E_1$) and a three-torus with a quarter turn ($E_3$) - the three-dimensional density field carries enough information to detect topology on scales up to 25 percent larger than those accessible from the two-dimensional cosmic microwave background anisotropies alone. Future probes of the cosmic density field using deep galaxy surveys or neutral-hydrogen 21-cm intensity mapping, combined with computationally intensive searches over the large parameter space of admissible topologies, thus offer a plausible avenue to extending the range of detectable cosmic topologies.

AI.tldr: The paper derives the covariance between perturbation modes in a universe with a compact spatial topology and uses this to estimate information about cosmic topology contained in the observable 3D density field. For two Euclidean examples (E1 cubic three-torus and E3 three-torus with quarter turn), the 3D density field can detect topology on scales up to 25% larger than from CMB anisotropies alone, suggesting deep galaxy surveys and 21-cm intensity mapping offer a viable path to extending detectable cosmic topology scales.
AI.motivation: To determine whether the three-dimensional cosmic density field observed by galaxy surveys and 21-cm intensity mapping can detect compact spatial topology at scales beyond what is accessible from CMB anisotropies, thereby extending the range of detectable cosmic topologies.
AI.method: The authors derive the covariance between perturbation modes in the full topology volume and compute the induced covariance between modes in the observable subvolume. They use this covariance to estimate the information about topology contained in the full set of observable linear perturbations, applied to two Euclidean examples: the cubic three-torus (E1) and a three-torus with a quarter turn (E3).
AI.result: For both sample Euclidean topologies (E1 and E3), the three-dimensional density field carries sufficient information to detect topology on scales up to 25 percent larger than those accessible from two-dimensional CMB anisotropies alone.
AI.conclusion: Future probes of the cosmic density field—through deep galaxy surveys or neutral-hydrogen 21-cm intensity mapping—combined with computationally intensive searches over the parameter space of admissible topologies, offer a plausible avenue to extending the range of detectable cosmic topologies.

title: The ionizing properties of JWST's compact broad-line emitters
comment: Main text 19 pages, 14 figures. Submitted to A&A. Comments are welcome
summary: The recent JWST discovery of a numerous population of broad-line emitters (BLEs) at $z>4$ has reopened the question of whether sources other than faint galaxies contributed significantly to cosmic reionization. To assess this contribution, we present a systematic census of compact, blue broad-line emitters at $4\leq z\leq7$ selected from the DJA, designed to isolate sources in which the UV continuum and the broad-line emission originate from the same compact physical region. Starting from a parent sample of 4145 galaxies with NIRSpec/PRISM spectroscopy and NIRCam imaging, we apply criteria on broad Ha emission (FWHM$>2000$km s-1, detected at S/N$\geq5$, complete at $L_{Ha,broad}\geq10^{42.7}$erg s-1), blue continuum slopes ($β_{UV}\leq-1.5$, $β_{opt}<0.5$), and morphological compactness in both the rest-frame UV and optical, returning a final sample of 20 sources. This constitutes $\sim20%$ of the PRISM-selected broad-line sample, which is dominated by Little Red Dots (LRDs). We find that the compact blue BLEs display hot ionizing continua, high-ionization UV lines (CIV, NIV], HeII), and elevated Lya emitter fractions ($X_{Lya}=50-67%$) relative to star-forming galaxies and LRDs. Beyond their similar lack of X-ray emission, their optical spectra closely resemble those of LRDs. This suggests that compact blue BLEs extend this population towards lower column density envelopes, but with similar engines, rather than representing a physically distinct population. Using Sirocco to model physical configurations that reproduce the observed spectra, we find a high ionizing photon production efficiency (log$ξ_{ion}\sim25.4$Hz erg-1) and a weighted average escape fraction $fesc\sim0.2$ for the bluest sources, and $\sim0.01$ for LRDs. This implies that broad-line sources do not dominate reionization globally, but given their luminosity, their contribution can dominate up to few Mpc scales.

AI.tldr: This paper conducts a systematic census of compact, blue broad-line emitters (BLEs) at 4≤z≤7 from the DJA spectroscopic survey, identifying 20 sources (~20% of PRISM-selected BLEs, most of which are Little Red Dots). These compact blue BLEs show hot ionizing continua, high-ionization UV lines, and high Lyman-alpha emitter fractions, and their optical spectra closely resemble LRDs despite having bluer colors. Spectral modeling yields high ionizing photon production efficiency (logξ_ion~25.4) with escape fractions of ~0.2 for the bluest sources and ~0.01 for LRDs, implying that broad-line sources do not dominate cosmic reionization globally but can dominate locally on few-Mpc scales.
AI.motivation: The JWST discovery of numerous broad-line emitters at z>4 raises the question of whether sources beyond faint galaxies contributed significantly to cosmic reionization. This paper aims to assess that contribution by systematically identifying and characterizing compact, blue BLEs—sources where the UV continuum and broad-line emission arise from the same compact region—and quantifying their ionizing photon production and escape fractions.
AI.method: Starting from 4145 galaxies with NIRSpec/PRISM spectroscopy and NIRCam imaging from the DJA, the authors apply selection criteria on broad Hα emission (FWHM>2000 km/s, S/N≥5, L_Hα,broad≥10^42.7 erg/s), blue continuum slopes (β_UV≤−1.5, β_opt<0.5), and morphological compactness in rest-frame UV and optical. The final sample of 20 compact blue BLEs is compared to LRDs and star-forming galaxies via spectral properties, and the Sirocco radiative transfer code is used to model the physical configurations and derive ionizing photon production efficiency and escape fractions.
AI.result: The sample comprises 20 compact blue BLEs, ~20% of the PRISM-selected broad-line population (dominated by LRDs). These sources display hot ionizing continua, high-ionization UV lines (CIV, NIV], HeII), and elevated Lyα emitter fractions (X_Lya=50–67%). Their optical spectra closely resemble LRDs, suggesting they extend the LRD population toward lower column density envelopes with similar central engines. Modeling yields logξ_ion~25.4 Hz erg−1 and a weighted average fesc~0.2 for the bluest sources, versus ~0.01 for LRDs.
AI.conclusion: Broad-line sources do not dominate cosmic reionization globally. However, given their luminosity, their contribution can dominate ionizing photon budgets on spatial scales up to a few Mpc. Compact blue BLEs are likely a low-column-density extension of the LRD population rather than a physically distinct source class.

title: The optimal redshift for dark energy I: formalism and interpretation
summary: We introduce the concept of the optimal redshift for dark energy, a statistically motivated redshift at which departures of the dark-energy equation of state (EOS) from the cosmological-constant value are tested most effectively. Within a generalized CPL parameterization, we derive an analytic expression for the optimal redshift by maximizing the separation of the EOS from $w=-1$ relative to the corresponding uncertainty. We establish the optimal redshift relationship to the phantom-crossing and pivot redshifts. As an illustration, we apply the formalism to the dataset combination of DESI DR2 BAO measurements, the DES Year-6 independent BAO measurement, and the recalibrated DES-Dovekie supernova sample. Adopting the null hypothesis $\mathcal{H}_0:w(a_{\rm opt})=-1$, we find a tension of ~$2.8σ$ with the cosmological-constant prediction at the optimal redshift, compared with ~$2.6σ$ at the pivot redshift, despite the latter having a smaller EOS uncertainty. This behavior reflects the specific design of the optimal redshift to maximize the statistical significance of a departure of the EOS from the -1 value of the $Λ$CDM model. We further provide statistical and geometrical interpretations of the optimum. In the CPL parameter space, the pivot corresponds to the projection that minimizes the variance of the equation of state, whereas the optimum maximizes its squared-distance from the cosmological-constant value over its variance. While the optimum is dataset and parameterization dependent, the underlying optimization principle and definition of the optimal redshift can be extended beyond the CPL framework. Future applications to DESI, Rubin LSST, Euclid, Roman Space Telescope, and other Stage-IV dark-energy surveys appear particularly promising.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the concept of an "optimal redshift" for dark energy—a statistically motivated redshift that maximizes the sensitivity of tests for deviations of the dark-energy equation of state (EOS) from w=-1 (the cosmological constant value). Using a CPL parameterization, the authors derive an analytic expression for this optimal redshift, relate it to the pivot and phantom-crossing redshifts, and apply it to DESI DR2 BAO + DES Y6 BAO + DES-Dovekie supernova data. They find a ~2.8σ tension with ΛCDM at the optimal redshift (vs ~2.6σ at the pivot redshift) and provide statistical and geometrical interpretations of the optimum, which generalizes beyond CPL to future Stage-IV surveys.
AI.motivation: To identify the redshift at which dark-energy equation-of-state departures from w=-1 can be tested with maximum statistical significance, thereby improving the design and interpretation of cosmological datasets probing dark energy dynamics.
AI.method: Within the generalized CPL parameterization, the authors maximize the ratio of EOS departure from w=-1 to its uncertainty to derive an analytic expression for the optimal redshift. They connect it to phantom-crossing and pivot redshifts and apply the formalism to combined DESI DR2 BAO, DES Y6 BAO, and recalibrated DES-Dovekie supernova data, testing the null hypothesis w(a_opt)=-1.
AI.result: A ~2.8σ tension with the cosmological-constant prediction is found at the optimal redshift, exceeding the ~2.6σ seen at the pivot redshift despite the latter's smaller EOS uncertainty. Geometrically, the pivot minimizes EOS variance while the optimum maximizes squared-distance from w=-1 over variance in the CPL parameter space.
AI.conclusion: The optimal redshift provides a more powerful statistical framework than the pivot redshift for detecting EOS deviations from ΛCDM. The principle is dataset and parameterization-dependent but generalizable, with promising applications to upcoming Stage-IV dark-energy surveys (DESI, Rubin LSST, Euclid, Roman).

title: To be lensed or not to be lensed: on the nature of the alleged high-z lensed quasars J0109-5424 and P170+20
comment: Accepted for publication in the Astrophysical Journal, 10 pages, 4 figures
summary: We present a detailed multi-wavelength analysis of two gravitationally lensed z>6 quasar candidates: J0109-5424 and P170+20. Using JWST/NIRSpec near-infrared data from the Aether survey, we demonstrate that J0109-5424 is in fact a FeLoBAL quasar at z=2.07, exhibiting strong iron broad absorption lines that mimic the Lyman break. From the Pabeta emission line, we estimate a black hole mass of 3.9 x 10^8 Msun and a bolometric luminosity of Lbol = 7.7 x 10^45 erg/s for this quasar. Follow-up HST/ACS WFC imaging of P170+20 with the F555W filter, probing emission below the Lyman limit of the quasar, reveals a compact source located 0.09+/-0.04 arcsec from the quasar position. PSF modelling and subtraction yield no evidence for extended emission. This is inconsistent with a foreground galaxy acting as a lens. Furthermore, we obtain Gemini-South/Flamingos 2 near-infrared observations to complement the existing optical Gemini-North/GMOS spectrum of P170+20. Our spectral analysis shows that the observed spectral shape of P170+20 is consistent with a composite quasar and M-dwarf spectrum. However, this interpretation remains uncertain, as a chance alignment between an ultracool dwarf and a quasar within 0.1 arcsec would be unlikely. Overall, our findings establish J0109-5424 as an intermediate redshift source and do not favor the lensed nature of P170+20, although this possibility cannot be conclusively ruled out, highlighting the challenges of selecting lensed quasars at high redshift.

AI.tldr: Multi-wavelength analysis of two z>6 lensed quasar candidates (J0109-5424 and P170+20) reveals that J0109-5424 is a FeLoBAL quasar at z=2.07 with black hole mass 3.9e8 Msun and bolometric luminosity 7.7e45 erg/s, while P170+20 shows no evidence for lensing from imaging and spectroscopy, with a spectral shape consistent with a quasar+M-dwarf coincidence, though this interpretation is uncertain.
AI.motivation: To verify and characterize two gravitationally lensed quasar candidates at z>6, addressing the reliability of high-redshift lensed quasar selection and the challenges in confirming lensing at high redshift.
AI.method: JWST/NIRSpec spectroscopy from the Aether survey for J0109-5424; HST/ACS WFC F555W imaging with PSF modeling/subtraction for P170+20; Gemini-South/Flamingos 2 near-infrared spectroscopy combined with existing Gemini-North/GMOS optical data for P170+20; spectral decomposition and black hole mass/luminosity estimation from emission lines.
AI.result: J0109-5424 is a FeLoBAL quasar at z=2.07 with M_BH=3.9e8 Msun and Lbol=7.7e45 erg/s, with iron BALs mimicking the Lyman break. P170+20 shows a compact source 0.09+/-0.04 arcsec from the quasar with no extended emission (inconsistent with a foreground lensing galaxy), and its spectral shape is consistent with a composite quasar+M-dwarf spectrum, though a chance alignment is unlikely.
AI.conclusion: J0109-5424 is an intermediate-redshift interloper, not a z>6 lensed quasar. P170+20 is not favored as lensed, though not conclusively ruled out. The study highlights significant challenges in identifying genuine lensed quasars at high redshift.

title: The optimal redshift for dark energy II: application to cosmological data and the evidence for the phantom crossing of the CPL equation of state
summary: Recent results from DESI and other cosmological datasets have indicated a preference for dynamical dark energy, with a time-evolving equation of state (EOS), $w(z)$. Furthermore, analyses using the CPL parameterization give an EOS with a phantom crossing of the $w(z)=-1$ line. In a companion paper-I, we assumed the CPL parameterization and its generalization, and introduced the formalism of the optimal scale factor (or redshift), a quantity designed to simultaneously maximize the distance from the cosmological constant value of $-1$ and to minimize the uncertainty on the EOS, thereby maximizing the tension with the cosmological constant at that specific redshift for a given dataset combination. In this paper-II, we apply the optimal-redshift formalism to available baryon acoustic oscillation, Cosmic Microwave Background, and supernova dataset combinations, with a particular focus on the phantom-line crossing within CPL. Motivated by the relatively low significance of previous constraints on the EOS in the region below the phantom line, we calculate the optimal redshift for a variety of dataset combinations to identify those that best constrain departures from $w(z)=-1$ before and after the crossing. We find combinations and corresponding optimal redshifts for which $w(z)$ lies below the ``$-1$'' line with new significance levels reaching $3.01$--$3.22σ$ before the crossing point, and $3.30$--$3.55σ$ above ``$-1$" after the crossing. Our focus in this work is the application of a new framework that maximizes the significance of the phantom-crossing signal within CPL using currently available datasets. Determining whether this crossing is effective or intrinsic, and identifying the underlying microphysical models, constitute separate questions from the aim of the present work and remain important directions for future investigation, further motivated by our findings. Abridged.

AI.tldr: The paper applies a novel "optimal redshift" framework to current cosmological datasets (BAO, CMB, supernovae) to maximize the significance of a dynamical dark energy signature—specifically a phantom crossing of the w(z)=-1 line within the CPL parameterization. The authors identify dataset combinations where the equation of state departs from -1 with significance levels of 3.01–3.22σ before the crossing and 3.30–3.55σ after it.
AI.motivation: Recent DESI and other cosmological data suggest dynamical dark energy with a time-evolving equation of state, including a possible phantom crossing of w(z)=-1. Previous constraints on the EOS below the phantom line have relatively low significance, so there is a need to identify which dataset combinations best constrain departures from w(z)=-1 around the crossing and maximize the statistical significance of this potential signal.
AI.method: The paper builds on a companion work (paper-I) that introduced the "optimal scale factor (or redshift)" formalism—a quantity designed to simultaneously maximize the distance from the cosmological constant value of -1 and minimize the uncertainty on the EOS. In this paper-II, this optimal-redshift framework is applied to various combinations of baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO), Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB), and supernova datasets, with a focus on the phantom-line crossing within the CPL parameterization.
AI.result: The authors identify dataset combinations and corresponding optimal redshifts for which the EOS lies below the -1 line with new significance levels reaching 3.01–3.22σ before the crossing point, and 3.30–3.55σ above -1 after the crossing—significantly improving over previous low-significance constraints.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates the utility of the optimal-redshift framework for maximizing the significance of phantom-crossing signals within CPL using currently available datasets. However, determining whether the crossing is effective (apparent) or intrinsic, and identifying the underlying microphysical models, remains separate from this paper's aim and is left for future investigation.

title: Tracing Galaxy Bias Through the Cosmic Web: The Role of Filaments
summary: The large-scale clustering of galaxies depends not only on their internal properties but also on their location within the cosmic web, which defines the anisotropic environments where galaxies form and evolve. Filaments serve as bridges through which galaxies and dark matter flow from low-density regions toward the highest-density nodes. In this work, we aim to map galaxy bias, which quantifies how these tracers follow the underlying dark matter density field, through the cosmic web, with a special emphasis on filaments. We look for dependencies on filament properties, such as length and density, and characterize the spatial variations of the large-scale bias along the filamentary spine. We applied the DisPerSE algorithm to identify the cosmic web in the TNG300 volume of the IllustrisTNG simulation. To measure large-scale galaxy bias, we utilized an object-by-object estimator, which provides advantages over standard estimators. We find that galaxies in node outskirts exhibit the highest large-scale bias values, reaching up to $\sim4$ times the values expected from theoretical models based on halo mass alone. Low-mass red galaxies in filaments and filament outskirts also display enhanced bias, which is strongly reduced after excluding galaxies close to nodes. Together, these results suggest that proximity to massive nodes plays a central role in shaping environmental secondary bias. Furthermore, galaxy bias decreases with filament length, from mean values of $1.4$ for short filaments to $-0.5$ for longer structures. This relation persists at fixed halo mass and galaxy color, and is not primarily driven by the average local galaxy density of the filament. Finally, short filaments exhibit an approximately uniform longitudinal bias profile, whereas long filaments show an increase in normalized bias from $\sim0.85$ near the saddle point to $\sim1.06$ close to the node.

AI.tldr: Using the IllustrisTNG300 simulation and the DisPerSE algorithm to identify the cosmic web, this paper maps galaxy bias through cosmic web structures (especially filaments). They find galaxies near nodes have the highest large-scale bias (up to 4× theoretical halo-mass-only values), low-mass red galaxies in filaments show enhanced bias, bias decreases with filament length (from ~1.4 to -0.5), and long filaments show increasing normalized bias from saddle point to node.
AI.motivation: To understand how the anisotropic cosmic web environments, particularly filaments, shape galaxy bias—which quantifies how galaxies trace the underlying dark matter density field—and to identify which filament properties (length, density) and spatial positions drive variations in large-scale bias.
AI.method: Applied the DisPerSE algorithm to identify the cosmic web in the TNG300 volume of the IllustrisTNG simulation, and used an object-by-object estimator to measure large-scale galaxy bias, which offers advantages over standard estimators.
AI.result: Galaxies in node outskirts reach up to ~4× higher bias than halo-mass-only theoretical predictions. Low-mass red galaxies in filaments and filament outskirts show enhanced bias, but this is strongly reduced when excluding galaxies near nodes. Galaxy bias decreases with filament length from ~1.4 (short filaments) to -0.5 (long filaments), persisting at fixed halo mass and color. Short filaments show uniform longitudinal bias profiles, while long filaments increase from ~0.85 near saddle points to ~1.06 near nodes.
AI.conclusion: Proximity to massive nodes is central to shaping environmental secondary bias. Filament length systematically affects galaxy bias independently of halo mass, galaxy color, and local density, revealing a spatially varying bias structure along the filamentary spine that is more pronounced in longer filaments.

title: Distinguishing cold and self-interacting dark matter through topological analysis
summary: Alternative dark matter (DM) models have emerged to solve the challenges faced by the predictions of collisionless cold dark matter (CDM) on galactic scales ($\lesssim 1\Mpc$). However, disentangling alternative models from CDM is difficult on such small scales because of the degeneracy with baryonic physics. It is therefore necessary to use DM probes that are not affected by baryons, e.g.\ that stand on intermediate scales, larger than galactic while remaining smaller than the scale at which the models converge to CDM. For the first time, we distinguish self-interacting DM (SIDM) from CDM using the genus statistic, a metric that characterises the topology of the density field. We carried out the analysis on the Darkium DM-only cosmological simulations, using one CDM model and four SIDM models with cross-sections of various amplitudes and velocity dependencies. We computed the genus on selected 3-virial radius wide regions centred around halos, for few hundred halos with masses ranging from $10^{12}$ to $10^{14}$ M$_\odot/h$ over redshifts $z=0$ to $z=2$. We also explored a more observation-like configuration, where the DM density field is traced only from the halo distribution in thick 2D projection since in principle redshift errors hinder a 3D reconstruction of the density field. We find that the density field is systematically clumpier in CDM than in SIDM models up to $0.05~\mathrm{Mpc}/h$, for halos of masses larger than $10^{12}\Msol/h$ at $z=0$. These predictions show that the genus of the density field is sensitive to DM self-interactions, suggesting that topological analysis could provide a valuable probe for distinguishing SIDM from CDM in observed halo distributions.

AI.tldr: The paper uses the genus statistic, a topological metric of the density field, to distinguish self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) from cold dark matter (CDM) for the first time. Using Darkium DM-only simulations with four SIDM models and one CDM model, the authors find that the density field is systematically clumpier in CDM than in SIDM for halos above 10^12 Msol/h at z=0, suggesting topological analysis as a promising probe for distinguishing DM models in observed halo distributions.
AI.motivation: Alternative dark matter models (e.g., SIDM) aim to solve the small-scale challenges faced by collisionless CDM predictions on galactic scales, but they are degenerate with baryonic physics on those scales. Therefore, the authors seek DM probes on intermediate scales—larger than galactic yet smaller than convergence scales—that are free from baryonic contamination to distinguish alternative models from CDM.
AI.method: The authors apply the genus statistic—a topological descriptor of the density field—to DM-only Darkium cosmological simulations. They analyze one CDM model and four SIDM models with varying cross-sections and velocity dependencies. The genus is computed on 3-virial-radius regions around a few hundred halos (10^12 to 10^14 Msol/h) across redshifts z=0 to z=2. They also test an observation-like configuration where the density field is traced from halo distributions in thick 2D projections to account for redshift errors hindering 3D reconstruction.
AI.result: The density field is systematically clumpier in CDM than in SIDM models up to 0.05 Mpc/h, for halos with masses larger than 10^12 Msol/h at z=0. This demonstrates that the genus statistic is sensitive to dark matter self-interactions.
AI.conclusion: The genus of the density field is sensitive to DM self-interactions, and topological analysis could provide a valuable observational probe for distinguishing SIDM from CDM in halo distributions.

title: A systematic study of AGN feedback in a disk galaxy using MACER. III. High Gas Fractions in AGN Hosts
comment: 14 pages, 9 figures. To be submitted to ApJ
summary: We use high-resolution hydrodynamic simulations in the MACER framework to explain why low-redshift PG quasar hosts can retain substantial cold-gas reservoirs, with gas fractions and gas-to-stellar mass ratios showing little dependence on instantaneous AGN luminosity. This paper is the third in a series systematically studying AGN feedback in a disk galaxy subject to cosmological gas inflow. The simulations include multiphase gas, star formation, stellar feedback, and self-consistent radiative and mechanical AGN feedback. We reproduce the observed weak connection between host-galaxy gas content and AGN luminosity over L_AGN/L_Edd ~ 10^{-5}-10, while the galaxy nevertheless undergoes pronounced gas depletion and star-formation quenching. During the quenching phase, the cold-gas mass declines by nearly three orders of magnitude, and the evolution of the gas distribution shows that AGN feedback progressively removes both cold and hot gas from the galaxy. The star formation rate is more closely linked to the cold-gas mass than to AGN luminosity. This behavior arises from a timescale mismatch: AGN luminosity varies on ~ 10^5-10^6 yr timescales, whereas repeated AGN-driven outflows cumulatively deplete the galaxy-scale gas reservoir over ~ 1 Gyr. Our simulations therefore provide a physical explanation for the gas-rich PG quasar hosts and show that their observed gas properties are fully consistent with effective, long-term ejective AGN feedback.

AI.tldr: Using high-resolution MACER hydrodynamic simulations, this paper explains why low-redshift PG quasar hosts retain substantial cold-gas reservoirs despite active AGN feedback. The weak correlation between host gas content and instantaneous AGN luminosity arises from a timescale mismatch: AGN luminosity fluctuates on ~10^5-10^6 yr timescales, while AGN-driven outflows cumulatively deplete the galaxy-scale gas over ~1 Gyr. The simulations reproduce observed gas fractions and demonstrate that gas-rich PG hosts are fully consistent with effective long-term ejective AGN feedback.
AI.motivation: To explain the puzzling observation that low-redshift PG quasar hosts have substantial cold-gas reservoirs with gas fractions largely independent of instantaneous AGN luminosity, despite expectations that AGN feedback should deplete gas.
AI.method: High-resolution hydrodynamic simulations in the MACER framework, including multiphase gas, star formation, stellar feedback, and self-consistent radiative and mechanical AGN feedback, applied to a disk galaxy subject to cosmological gas inflow.
AI.result: The simulations reproduce the weak connection between host-galaxy gas content and AGN luminosity over L_AGN/L_Edd ~ 10^-5-10. During quenching, cold-gas mass declines by nearly three orders of magnitude as AGN feedback progressively removes both cold and hot gas. Star formation rate correlates more closely with cold-gas mass than AGN luminosity.
AI.conclusion: The observed gas-rich PG quasar hosts are physically explained by a timescale mismatch between rapid AGN luminosity variability (10^5-10^6 yr) and cumulative long-term (~1 Gyr) gas depletion by AGN-driven outflows. These gas properties are fully consistent with effective, long-term ejective AGN feedback.

title: Constraining primordial non-Gaussianity and energy injection with the thermal Sunyaev-Zeldovich effect and integrated Sachs-Wolfe effect cross-correlation
summary: Constraining primordial non-Gaussianity (PNG) provides key insights into the physics of cosmic inflation and the initial conditions of the Universe, which remain central topics in cosmology. In this study, we use the cross-correlation between the integrated Sachs-Wolfe (ISW) effect and the thermal Sunyaev-Zeldovich (tSZ) effect derived from Ibitoye et al. (2024) to jointly constrain PNG and early-Universe energy injection, including the standard intergalactic medium contribution. For scale-independent PNG we obtain $f_{\rm NL} = -358^{+140}_{-114}$ ($68\%$~C.L.). For a scale-dependent model ($f_{\rm NL}=f_{\rm NL}^{0}(\ell/\ell_{0})^{n_{\rm NL}}$, with $\ell_{0}=200$), we find $f^{0}_{\rm NL} = -296^{+173}_{-157}$ and $n_{\rm NL} = 0.62^{+1.02}_{-0.64}$, both consistent with Gaussian initial conditions. We also constrain the early-Universe energy injection amplitude to be $α_{\rm inj} = -3.93^{+1.34}_{-0.99}$, with uncertainty reduced by a factor of $\sim\!2.6$ if Planck 2018 $f_{\rm NL}$ constraint is applied as a prior. Future surveys such as Simons Observatory and Euclid will tighten these constraints further. Complementary to conventional probes, this work provides the first ISW-tSZ constraint on exotic energy injection and enables precision tests of early-Universe physics while probing late-time gravitational potential and thermal energy perturbations.

AI.tldr: The paper uses the cross-correlation between the integrated Sachs-Wolfe (ISW) effect and the thermal Sunyaev-Zeldovich (tSZ) effect to jointly constrain primordial non-Gaussianity (PNG) and early-Universe energy injection, finding f_NL = -358^{+140}_{-114} for scale-independent PNG, constraints on scale-dependent PNG consistent with Gaussian initial conditions, and an energy injection amplitude α_inj = -3.93^{+1.34}_{-0.99}, with the first ISW-tSZ constraint on exotic energy injection.
AI.motivation: Constraining primordial non-Gaussianity provides key insights into the physics of cosmic inflation and the initial conditions of the Universe, which are central topics in cosmology. The study aims to simultaneously constrain PNG and early-Universe energy injection using a complementary observational probe (ISW-tSZ cross-correlation).
AI.method: The study uses the cross-correlation between the integrated Sachs-Wolfe (ISW) effect and the thermal Sunyaev-Zeldovich (tSZ) effect derived from Ibitoye et al. (2024). It jointly constrains PNG (both scale-independent and scale-dependent models) and early-Universe energy injection, including the standard intergalactic medium contribution. A Planck 2018 f_NL prior is also applied to assess its impact on the energy injection constraint.
AI.result: For scale-independent PNG, f_NL = -358^{+140}_{-114} (68% C.L.). For a scale-dependent model, f^0_NL = -296^{+173}_{-157} and n_NL = 0.62^{+1.02}_{-0.64}, both consistent with Gaussian initial conditions. The early-Universe energy injection amplitude is α_inj = -3.93^{+1.34}_{-0.99}, with uncertainty reduced by ~2.6 when applying the Planck 2018 f_NL prior.
AI.conclusion: The work provides the first ISW-tSZ constraint on exotic energy injection and enables precision tests of early-Universe physics while probing late-time gravitational potential and thermal energy perturbations. Future surveys such as Simons Observatory and Euclid are expected to tighten these constraints further, demonstrating the ISW-tSZ cross-correlation as a complementary probe to conventional methods.

title: Laplace surface of eccentric orbits around Kerr black hole and black-hole effects on Lidov-Kozai cycles
summary: We study the Laplace surface of eccentric orbits around a Kerr black hole with a companion star. The two relativistic effects (periapsis apsidal precession and Lense-Thirring precession) balance companion's tidal effect. By solving the secular equations, we find that the two branches of equilibrium solutions exist only in a narrow range of orbital inclinations of test particle, and that the stability exists when companion's obliquity approaches 90 degree. We then study the black-hole effects on Lidov-Kozai cycles. In addition to the black-hole suppression on cycle amplitude, we find that the cycle frequency is non-monotonic about distance from black hole and reaches its minimum in the transition between GR apsidal precession and companions's tidal precession. Finally we use this mechanism to well interpret the nearly isotropic orientation of S-cluster in the Galactic center.

AI.tldr: The paper studies the Laplace surface of eccentric orbits around a Kerr black hole with a companion star, showing that relativistic effects (apsidal and Lense-Thirring precession) balance the companion's tidal effect. It finds two equilibrium branches exist only in a narrow orbital inclination range with stability near 90-degree companion obliquity, analyzes black-hole effects on Lidov-Kozai cycles (including non-monotonic frequency), and applies this to explain the nearly isotropic orientation of S-cluster in the Galactic center.
AI.motivation: To understand how relativistic effects around a rotating (Kerr) black hole interact with a companion star's tidal forces, and to explain the observed nearly isotropic orbital orientation of the S-cluster stars near the Galactic center.
AI.method: The authors solve secular equations describing the balance between relativistic precession (periapsis apsidal precession and Lense-Thirring precession) and the companion star's tidal precession, analyzing equilibrium Laplace surfaces, their stability, and the resulting modifications to Lidov-Kozai cycles.
AI.result: Two branches of Laplace-surface equilibrium solutions exist only in a narrow range of test-particle orbital inclinations; stability occurs when the companion's obliquity approaches 90 degrees. Black-hole effects damp Lidov-Kozai cycle amplitude, and the cycle frequency is non-monotonic with distance from the black hole, reaching a minimum at the transition between GR apsidal precession and companion tidal precession. This mechanism successfully interprets the nearly isotropic orientation of the S-cluster.
AI.conclusion: The combination of Kerr black-hole relativistic precessions and a companion's tidal field shapes the Laplace surface geometry and Lidov-Kozai dynamics in specific ways, and this framework provides a compelling explanation for the near-isotropic orbital orientation observed in the Galactic center S-cluster.

title: Filaments within filaments: unraveling the hierarchy of the cosmic web
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures, prepared for submission to PRL
summary: Cosmic filaments are the most striking feature of the hierarchical cosmic web. Yet, their own sub-structure remains unexplored, unlike the well-known, universal halo/sub-halo hierarchy. We use a hierarchical reconstruction scheme to identify sub-filaments within larger filaments. Examining differences in the radial phase-space profiles of parent and sub-filaments, we argue that the latter constitute a statistically distinct class of structures. Establishing the existence of a universal filament hierarchy must then account for these differences, with implications for cosmology and dark matter.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies and analyzes sub-filaments within larger cosmic filaments using a hierarchical reconstruction scheme, showing that parent and sub-filaments have distinct radial phase-space profiles, establishing sub-filaments as a statistically separate class of structures with cosmological implications.
AI.motivation: While the hierarchical cosmic web structure is well-known, the sub-structure within cosmic filaments has remained unexplored, unlike the extensively studied halo/sub-halo hierarchy. The authors aim to investigate whether filaments possess their own internal hierarchy.
AI.method: The authors apply a hierarchical reconstruction scheme to identify sub-filaments nested within larger filaments, then compare the radial phase-space profiles of parent filaments versus sub-filaments to assess whether they form statistically distinct classes of structures.
AI.result: The analysis reveals differences in radial phase-space profiles between parent and sub-filaments, indicating that sub-filaments constitute a statistically distinct class of structures rather than simple scaled-down versions of their parents.
AI.conclusion: Any claim of a universal filament hierarchy must account for these observed differences between parent and sub-filaments. This has implications for cosmological models and our understanding of dark matter distribution in the cosmic web.

title: Recovering the effective impact parameters in integral-field absorption-line tomography
summary: Integral-field-unit (IFU) spectroscopy of extended background sources, such as gravitational arcs, delivers many closely spaced absorption sightlines through the circumgalactic medium (CGM) of foreground galaxies. However, the source extent and smearing through the point spread function (PSF) cause each spaxel to integrate light from a region larger than itself. The usually adopted geometric spaxel centre is therefore not representative of where the absorbed flux originates. Informed by high-resolution imaging, we introduce a flux-contribution formalism that reconstructs the spatial origin of the flux in each spaxel by defining flux-weighted coordinates and impact parameters. Using a data-driven simulation built on a real gravitational-arc configuration, we show that spaxel centres are displaced from the flux-weighted positions by $|Δ\mathbf{x}| \propto θ_{\rm PSF}(1-f)$, with $f$ the spaxel-source overlap fraction, and that the resulting impact-parameter bias scales with the lensing magnification as $μ^{-1/2}$. These offsets are largest for off-arc spaxels and flatten the radial column-density profiles. They also inject a coherent geometry-driven scatter that mimics intrinsic CGM structure and that is removed neither by a tighter spaxel selection nor by a finer spatial binning. For identical uncertainties, the spaxel-centre coordinates leave residuals of about twice the noise level ($χ^2_ν\sim 4$), whereas the flux-weighted coordinates recover the input profile to within the uncertainties ($χ^2_ν\sim 1$) and remain robust to a PSF misspecification of $\pm 10\%$. The method we propose provides a better-motivated and readily adoptable framework for tomographic studies, whether as the primary analysis or as a robustness check on spaxel-centre results.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a flux-contribution formalism for integral-field-unit (IFU) spectroscopy that reconstructs the true spatial origin of absorbed flux in each spaxel of extended background sources like gravitational arcs. The method uses flux-weighted coordinates and impact parameters, informed by high-resolution imaging, to correct biases introduced by the PSF and source extent. Simulations show this approach eliminates systematic impact-parameter bias (scaling as μ^{-1/2}), reduces residuals to within noise levels (χ²_ν~1 vs ~4 for spaxel-centre methods), and remains robust to ±10% PSF misspecification.
AI.motivation: In IFU spectroscopy of extended background sources, the geometric spaxel centre is not representative of where absorbed flux actually originates because the source extent and PSF smearing cause each spaxel to integrate light from a larger region. This creates systematic biases in impact-parameter measurements and introduces geometry-driven scatter that mimics intrinsic CGM structure, which cannot be removed by spaxel selection or finer binning.
AI.method: The authors propose a flux-contribution formalism that uses high-resolution imaging to define flux-weighted coordinates and impact parameters for each spaxel. They demonstrate the formalism using a data-driven simulation built on a real gravitational-arc configuration, quantifying the displacement between spaxel centres and flux-weighted positions and testing robustness to PSF misspecification.
AI.result: Spaxel centres are displaced from flux-weighted positions by |Δx| ∝ θ_PSF(1-f), with f the spaxel-source overlap fraction, and the impact-parameter bias scales with lensing magnification as μ^{-1/2}. Offsets are largest for off-arc spaxels and flatten radial column-density profiles. The flux-weighted coordinates recover input profiles within uncertainties (χ²_ν~1) while spaxel-centre coordinates leave residuals about twice the noise level (χ²_ν~4), and the method is robust to ±10% PSF misspecification.
AI.conclusion: The flux-weighted formalism provides a better-motivated and readily adoptable framework for tomographic CGM studies, useful either as the primary analysis method or as a robustness check on traditional spaxel-centre results.

title: An Inverse Lyth Bound for Non-Attractor Inflation
summary: I present a novel physics result generated entirely autonomously by ChatGPT 5.6 Sol. The Lyth bound relates an observable primordial tensor amplitude to a lower limit on the field excursion during single-field slow-roll inflation. We show that non-attractor evolution obeys a complementary upper bound. For a canonically normalized scalar field, the nonconstant superhorizon curvature mode is anti-damped whenever the second Hubble-flow parameter satisfies $ε_2\equiv d\lnε/dN<-3$. The same condition requires the inflaton kinetic energy to decrease sufficiently rapidly that the field-space distance traversed during a non-attractor interval obeys $Δφ_{\rm NA} / M_{\text{P}} < \left(2\sqrt{2ε_{\rm in}}/3\right) \left(1-e^{-3ΔN/2}\right) < \left(2\sqrt{2ε_{\rm in}}/3\right)$.The result is independent of the potential and does not require the slow-roll approximation. If $ε_2=-p<-3$ is constant, the stronger bound $Δφ/M_{\text{P}}<2\sqrt{2ε_{\rm in}}/p$ is saturated asymptotically. In ultra-slow-roll inflation, $p=6$, giving $Δφ<\sqrt{2ε_{\rm in}}M_{\text{P}}/3$. We derive an exact relation between field excursion and amplification of the velocity of the nonconstant curvature mode, and give the corresponding scalar-power relation in the quasi-de Sitter limit. In contrast with the usual Lyth relation, arbitrarily large non-attractor amplification approaches a finite field distance. This provides a model-independent field-range constraint on canonical single-field mechanisms for amplifying primordial fluctuations.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a novel physics result autonomously generated by ChatGPT 5.6 Sol, establishing an upper bound on the field excursion during non-attractor (ultra-slow-roll) inflation, complementing the well-known Lyth bound which provides a lower limit. For a canonical scalar field, when the second Hubble-flow parameter satisfies ε₂ < -3, the nonconstant superhorizon curvature mode is anti-damped, and the field-space distance traversed obeys Δφ/M_P < (2√(2ε_in)/3)(1-e^{-3ΔN/2}), independent of the potential. In ultra-slow-roll inflation (p=6), this gives Δφ < √(2ε_in)M_P/3. Unlike the Lyth relation, arbitrarily large non-attractor amplification approaches a finite field distance, providing a model-independent field-range constraint on canonical single-field inflationary mechanisms.
AI.motivation: The Lyth bound constrains the lower limit of field excursion during single-field slow-roll inflation given an observable primordial tensor amplitude. The authors aim to establish a complementary upper bound on field excursion for non-attractor evolution, which is important for understanding the field-range constraints on canonical single-field mechanisms for amplifying primordial fluctuations—particularly relevant for models producing primordial black holes or enhanced scalar power spectra.
AI.method: The analysis derives an upper bound on the field excursion during non-attractor inflation by analyzing the behavior of the nonconstant superhorizon curvature mode under the condition ε₂ < -3 (where ε₂ ≡ dlnε/dN is the second Hubble-flow parameter). The authors derive: (1) the anti-damping condition for the curvature mode, (2) an inequality relating field distance to initial ε (Δφ_NA/M_P < (2√(2ε_in)/3)(1-e^{-3ΔN/2})), which is potential-independent and does not require the slow-roll approximation, (3) a saturated asymptotic bound for constant ε₂=-p, yielding Δφ/M_P < 2√(2ε_in)/p, and (4) an exact relation between field excursion and velocity amplification of the curvature mode, with the corresponding scalar-power relation in the quasi-de Sitter limit.
AI.result: The key result is a complementary upper bound to the Lyth bound for non-attractor inflation: Δφ_NA/M_P < (2√(2ε_in)/3)(1-e^{-3ΔN/2}) < 2√(2ε_in)/3, which is independent of the potential and does not assume slow-roll. For constant ε₂=-p with p>3, the stronger bound Δφ/M_P < 2√(2ε_in)/p is saturated asymptotically. In ultra-slow-roll inflation (p=6), this yields Δφ < √(2ε_in)M_P/3. An exact relation between field excursion and curvature-mode velocity amplification is derived, and the scalar-power relation is given in the quasi-de Sitter limit. Unlike the Lyth relation where larger amplification requires larger field range, arbitrarily large non-attractor amplification approaches a finite field distance.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes a model-independent field-range constraint on canonical single-field inflation mechanisms that amplify primordial fluctuations via non-attractor dynamics. This upper bound complements the Lyth lower bound, showing that non-attractor evolution requires only finite (and often modest) field excursions regardless of amplification magnitude—a significant result for model building in inflationary cosmology.

title: Infrared photoprocessing of porous amorphous solid water with a free electron laser
comment: 14 pages, 7 figures in main text, 4 figures in Appendix
summary: Water ice is the most abundant ice in the interstellar medium (ISM). Previous studies on porous amorphous solid water (pASW) have shown that the infrared radiation field in the ISM modeled with infrared free electron laser (FEL) irradiation can result in changes in the ice towards a more ordered structure, characterized by a change in the OH-stretching vibration band. This paper aims to study the restructuring in more detail by varying the irradiation intensity and irradiation time for irradiations on-resonance with the OH-stretching, bending and libration modes. In addition, desorption of H2O is monitored during the irradiations. The research presented in this paper considers 42 infrared FEL irradiations on pASW samples deposited at two different rates, using the infrared FELs of the HFML-FELIX laboratory. Restructuring is studied using reflection absorption infrared (RAIR) spectroscopy, with a mass spectrometer monitoring the desorption of H2O in an ultra-high vacuum system. Desorption and restructuring occur in parallel, with the strongest effects observed for irradiation on-resonance with the OH-stretching vibration. Both processes exhibit two distinct regimes: an initial strong restructuring and desorption, characterized by an exponential decrease in the intensity of the desorption peaks within the first 5 s of irradiation, followed by a second regime of less efficient, yet continued restructuring and constant desorption in an extended area, involving energy dissipation through the hydrogen-bonding network. The trends in restructuring and desorption, depending on the absorbed energy during irradiation, are significantly different, suggesting separate processes. The astrophysical relevance of in particular the second regime of constant desorption and restructuring is discussed.

AI.tldr: This study uses infrared free electron laser irradiation on porous amorphous solid water (pASW) ice, varying intensity and time for on-resonance irradiation with OH-stretching, bending, and libration modes. Restructuring and H2O desorption occur in parallel with two distinct regimes—an initial strong exponential phase within 5 s, followed by a slower continued phase driven by energy dissipation through the hydrogen-bonding network. The astrophysical relevance of the second regime is discussed.
AI.motivation: To understand how the interstellar infrared radiation field restructures the most abundant interstellar ice (pASW) toward a more ordered structure, and to detail this restructuring by systematically varying irradiation intensity and time across different vibrational modes, while also monitoring H2O desorption.
AI.method: 42 infrared FEL irradiations on pASW samples deposited at two different rates, using the HFML-FELIX laboratory. Restructuring was probed via reflection absorption infrared (RAIR) spectroscopy, and H2O desorption was monitored with a mass spectrometer in an ultra-high vacuum system.
AI.result: Desorption and restructuring occur in parallel with strongest effects on-resonance with the OH-stretching vibration. Both processes show two regimes: an initial strong phase (exponential decrease of desorption peaks within 5 s) and a second, less efficient but continued phase with constant desorption driven by energy dissipation through the hydrogen-bonding network. Restructuring and desorption trends diverge with absorbed energy, indicating separate underlying processes.
AI.conclusion: The restructuring and desorption of pASW under infrared irradiation are distinct but parallel processes, each exhibiting a two-regime behavior. The sustained second regime of constant desorption and restructuring has significant astrophysical implications that are discussed.

title: Energetics of AGN Feedback
comment: 15 pages, 9 figures, 2 tables; accepted in MNRAS
summary: Integrating realistic active galactic nucleus (AGN) feedback into cosmological hydrodynamical simulations remains a major challenge as resolving the spatial coupling of jet energy over cosmic timescales is computationally prohibitive. We present an analytic framework that predicts the radial and polar-angle dependence of feedback energy from lobed AGNs, enabling a physically motivated, computationally efficient prescription for jet feedback. Built upon the Radio AGN in Semi-analytic Environments (RAiSE) dynamical model, our approach tracks the post-AGN jet phase evolution of radio sources through two distinct mechanisms: buoyantly rising bubbles subject to ablation, and the gravitational collapse of swept-up gas in the shocked shell. We find that these two feedback mechanisms produce strongly contrasting spatial distributions across ten representative cluster environments. Buoyant bubbles preferentially deposit energy in steep density gradients near the core radius, while the collapsing shocked gas shell drives heating within flatter cluster cores. Weak, short-lived AGN outbursts ($Q<10^{37}$ W and $t_{\rm on}<10$ Myr) confine their energy deposition to the inner 10 kpc of the cluster; longer-lived events ($t_{\rm on} \geqslant 100$ Myr) deposit less than 1% of their injected energy within 30 kpc. We find that time-averaged heating rates across multiple outbursts are sufficient to offset radiative cooling in all but the highest density cluster cores (within 100 kpc) for duty cycles of $0.08< δ\leqslant 1$. This framework provides a scalable basis for modelling anisotropic, physically motivated jet feedback that can be incorporated into next-generation cosmological simulations.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an analytic framework built on the RAiSE dynamical model to predict the spatial distribution of feedback energy from lobed AGNs, tracking both buoyant bubbles undergoing ablation and gravitational collapse of swept-up shocked gas. The framework shows contrasting energy deposition patterns across cluster environments, with buoyant bubbles depositing energy near the core radius in steep density gradients while collapsing shocked shells heat flatter cores. Time-averaged heating rates can offset radiative cooling in all but the densest cluster cores for duty cycles between 0.08 and 1, providing a scalable, physically motivated prescription for sub-grid jet feedback in cosmological simulations.
AI.motivation: Resolving the spatial coupling of AGN jet energy over cosmic timescales in cosmological hydrodynamical simulations is computationally prohibitive. There is a need for a physically motivated, computationally efficient prescription for jet feedback that captures realistic AGN energetics.
AI.method: The framework is built upon the Radio AGN in Semi-analytic Environments (RAiSE) dynamical model. It tracks post-AGN jet phase evolution through two distinct mechanisms: (1) buoyantly rising bubbles subject to ablation, and (2) gravitational collapse of swept-up gas in the shocked shell. The model predicts radial and polar-angle dependence of feedback energy and is tested across ten representative cluster environments.
AI.result: The two feedback mechanisms produce contrasting spatial distributions. Buoyant bubbles deposit energy preferentially in steep density gradients near the core radius, while collapsing shocked gas shells drive heating within flatter cluster cores. Weak, short-lived AGN outbursts (Q<10^37 W, t_on<10 Myr) confine energy to the inner 10 kpc; longer-lived events (t_on≥100 Myr) deposit less than 1% of injected energy within 30 kpc. Time-averaged heating rates offset radiative cooling in all but the highest density cluster cores within 100 kpc for duty cycles of 0.08<δ≤1.
AI.conclusion: This analytic framework provides a scalable basis for modelling anisotropic, physically motivated jet feedback and can be incorporated into next-generation cosmological simulations, addressing a key bottleneck in simulating realistic AGN feedback over cosmic timescales.

title: REBELS-25: multi-phase morphology and kinematics at z = 7.31
summary: We present a spatially resolved, multi-wavelength study of the massive, star-forming galaxy REBELS-25 at a redshift of $z=7.31$. We combine new high-resolution ALMA [O III]88$μ$m observations with resolution-matched [C II], dust continuum, and JWST/NIRSpec IFU spectroscopy, providing a $\lesssim1$ kpc view of the morphology, interstellar medium (ISM) conditions, and multi-tracer gas kinematics of one of the most mature galaxies known in the reionisation era. We find differing morphologies from the rest-frame UV to far-infrared (FIR) emission, with the UV and optical emission appearing clumpy and irregular, whereas the FIR emission is well-described by near-exponential disc profiles, with [C II] being the most extended. Comparing the resolved UV and FIR emission, we find that obscured star formation contributes $\sim55$-$98$% of the total star formation rate across the galaxy, demonstrating that dust obscuration strongly shapes the observed UV and optical morphology. Resolved ionisation-line diagnostics show no significant variation across the source at $\sim1$ kpc resolution, consistent with broadly similar ISM conditions among the identified regions. Overall, these results further support a picture in which REBELS-25 hosts a dusty, chemically enriched, and dynamically cold ISM already in place at $z=7.31$.

title: The Nobeyama 45 m Survey of Shocked Molecular Gas in the Central Molecular Zone. I. Survey Data, Cloud Catalog, and SiO Line-Ratio Trends
comment: Accepted for publication in ApJS. 36 pages, 27 figures, 4 tables. Calibrated FITS data products are available at doi:10.5281/zenodo.19588616
summary: We present large-scale molecular line maps of the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) in our Galaxy obtained with the Nobeyama Radio Observatory 45 m telescope. The observations cover a 3.5 deg x 0.5 deg region with 20 arcsec resolution in eight molecular lines including SiO J=2-1, CS J=2-1, H13CN J=1-0, and HCN J=1-0. We release the calibrated data cubes and a catalog of SiO-emitting clouds identified by the SCIMES algorithm. For each cloud, we provide cloud-integrated intensities of the observed lines and derive an H13CN-based molecular gas mass and a cloud-averaged H2 number density. We compare SiO intensity ratios with the density, dynamical time, and their product n_H2 t_dyn. We find that SiO intensity ratios relative to six other molecular lines all decrease systematically with increasing n_H2 t_dyn. The tightest correlations are found for SiO/H13CN (r_s = -0.82) and SiO/CS (r_s = -0.70). The released data cubes and cloud catalog enable systematic studies of SiO enhancement, shock chemistry, and gas dynamical evolution across the CMZ.

title: Revealing Galactic dust beneath the cosmic infrared background anisotropies with Wavelet Phase Harmonics
summary: Separating Galactic dust emission from cosmic infrared background (CIB) anisotropies is challenging because both the emission components have similar spectral properties. The primary objective of this work is to develop a component-separation algorithm to extract the Galactic dust emission from CIB anisotropies dominated sky regions using Wavelet Phase Harmonics statistics (WPH). We apply our algorithm to the \textit{Planck} $353\,\mathrm{GHz}$ frequency band over three sky regions spanning a range of neutral hydrogen ($\text{HI}$) column densities at high Galactic latitudes. In all three regions, we successfully recover the dust signal without significant leakage between the dust and CIB anisotropy components. We use the low signal-to-noise ($\mathrm{S/N}$) region to validate the component-separation algorithm and compare its performance with the standard template-fit approach that uses the linear dust-$\text{HI}$ correlation relation. For intermediate and high $\mathrm{S/N}$ regions, we separate the dust signal map from the contamination while preserving the statistical correlation with $\text{HI}$ column density map. Dust maps are used to analyze the relationship between dust and $\text{HI}$ emissions. We characterize the spatial variations in dust emission relative to the hydrogen column density as a function of the angular scale.

AI.method: The authors apply a Wavelet Phase Harmonics (WPH) statistics-based component-separation algorithm to Planck 353 GHz data over three high-latitude sky regions with a range of neutral hydrogen (HI) column densities. The algorithm is validated using a low signal-to-noise region and compared against the standard template-fit method based on linear dust-HI correlation.

title: Stellar mass growth in COSMOS-Web: a mass-complete main sequence to z ~ 8 and its consistency with GSMF evolution
comment: 14 pages, 5 figures, submitted to Astronomy & Astrophysics (A&A)
summary: The star-forming main sequence (MS) links the instantaneous star-formation rate of galaxies to their stellar-mass growth and therefore to the evolution of the galaxy stellar mass function (GSMF). We determine a mass-complete MS in COSMOS-Web out to z=8 and test whether its mass and redshift dependence is consistent with the observed evolution of the GSMF. We stacked 251,462 star-forming galaxies in Herschel and JCMT maps and corrected the far-infrared fluxes for blending using forward-modeled maps. We combined the resulting infrared luminosities with the unobscured ultraviolet emission to derive total star-formation rates and fitted a redshift-dependent MS. We independently measured the quiescent fraction and evolved the observed z=8 COSMOS-Web GSMF forward within a continuity-equation framework including stellar-mass return, suppression of in-situ growth by the quiescent fraction, and mergers. The MS is well described by a power law at low masses with a redshift-dependent turnover toward high masses. We measure a low-mass slope of gamma=1.215+/-0.028, implying a mildly increasing specific star-formation rate with stellar mass. The GSMF evolved using this relation follows the observed progressive flattening of the low-mass end substantially better than the literature MS prescriptions considered here. Mergers change the low-mass number densities by <=0.2 dex by z~0.65 and have little effect on the slope. Small differences in MS normalization also accumulate strongly, producing large differences in the evolved GSMF after several Gyr. The observed GSMF evolution provides an independent integral test of the MS. Our results favor a mildly super-linear low-mass MS and show that both its slope and normalization must be measured accurately to reproduce the buildup of the galaxy stellar-mass distribution.
